key_facts: Conus medullaris ends at L1/L2 (varies between T12-L2)
Cauda equina syndrome = bilateral leg pain, saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction
Emergency decompression needed within 48 hours for best neurological recovery
MRI is gold standard imaging
clinical_scenarios: Central disc herniation L4/5 with progressive paraparesis
Post-laminectomy spinal instability causing myelopathy
exam_pitfalls: Confusing conus with cauda equina presentation
Missing bilateral symptoms indicating central pathology

key_facts: C5-C6 (Erb's palsy): waiter's tip position, loss of abduction/external rotation
C8-T1 (Klumpke's palsy): claw hand, loss of intrinsic hand muscles
Root avulsion vs traction: myelography shows nerve root sleeves absent in avulsion
Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) indicates T1 root involvement
clinical_scenarios: Motorcycle crash with shoulder dislocation and C5/6 nerve injury
Birth injury with persistent Erb's palsy at 6 months
exam_pitfalls: Not testing intrinsic hand muscles in lower plexus injuries
Assuming all injuries are traction injuries (some are transection)

Applied Surgical Anatomy.concept: Femoral nerve anatomy and femoral block
key_facts: Femoral nerve posterior to femoral artery in groin (vein is medial)
Femoral block provides analgesia to: anterior thigh, knee, medial leg via saphenous nerve
Does NOT cover lateral thigh (lateral femoral cutaneous nerve separate)
Saphenous nerve block needed for medial lower leg
clinical_scenarios: Femoral fracture analgesia in trauma — femoral block before traction
Post-ACL repair analgesia
exam_pitfalls: Thinking femoral block covers whole leg (doesn't reach posterior thigh or calf)
Mistaking femoral vein anatomy — it's medial not lateral

key_facts: Negative intrathoracic pressure in inspiration sucks venous blood into right atrium
Positive pressure ventilation (IPPV) REDUCES venous return
In cardiac tamponade, venous return is mechanically obstructed despite intrathoracic pressure
Fluid responsiveness depends on Frank-Starling curve position
clinical_scenarios: Hypotensive patient on mechanical ventilation — reduce PEEP to improve VR
Cardiac tamponade with pulsus paradoxus (>10mmHg drop in SBP on inspiration)
exam_pitfalls: Thinking IPPV increases preload (it decreases it)
Confusing pulsus paradoxus with pulsus alternans

key_facts: DO2 = CO × Hb × SaO2 × 1.34 (+ dissolved O2)
VO2 = DO2 × (1 - SvO2) — extraction depends on capillary oxygen diffusion
Lactic acidosis suggests inadequate DO2 or mitochondrial dysfunction
Increasing FiO2 above PaO2 100 doesn't improve DO2 if Hb saturated
clinical_scenarios: Septic shock: high cardiac output, low SVR, high SvO2 ('cloud like' appearance on CXR)
Cardiogenic shock: low CO, high SVR, low SvO2
exam_pitfalls: Assuming normal SaO2 = adequate oxygenation (need DO2 and extraction)
Giving more oxygen in cardiogenic shock without inotropes

key_facts: Respiratory acidosis: hypercapnia (high CO2) — hypoventilation
Respiratory alkalosis: hypocapnia (low CO2) — hyperventilation
Metabolic acidosis: low HCO3 or high H+
Winter's formula: predicted pCO2 = 1.5×[HCO3] + 8 ±2 — if actual > predicted = concurrent respiratory acidosis
clinical_scenarios: Post-op respiratory depression with pCO2 55, pH 7.28, HCO3 24 → primary respiratory acidosis
Severe diarrhoea with pH 7.2, HCO3 12, pCO2 25 → metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
exam_pitfalls: Missing mixed disorders (calculating Winter's formula is key)
Not recognizing when respiratory compensation is INADEQUATE

key_facts: Haemostasis (0-10 min): platelets, fibrin clot
Inflammation (0-3 days): neutrophils, macrophages, cytokine release
Proliferation (3 days-3 weeks): fibroblasts, collagen I/III, angiogenesis, granulation tissue
Remodelling (3 weeks-2 years): collagen cross-linking, scar maturation, type I dominant
Collagen tensile strength at 2 weeks = ~30% of unwounded skin
clinical_scenarios: Acute inflammatory response after appendicectomy (fever, WCC rise expected)
Excessive scar tissue after deep burn — excessive collagen in remodelling phase
exam_pitfalls: Thinking healing is 'complete' after epithelialization (remodelling continues for months)
Not considering vitamin C/zinc/protein needs during proliferation phase

key_facts: Multi-hit hypothesis: typically 4-7 mutations for malignant transformation
Hallmarks: sustained proliferation, apoptosis evasion, replicative immortality, angiogenesis, invasion/metastasis
Epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT): loss of E-cadherin, gain of vimentin → increased motility
Lymphatic spread earlier than vascular for most solid tumours
clinical_scenarios: Colorectal cancer: APC → KRAS → TP53 → SMAD4 sequence over 10-15 years
Invasive ductal carcinoma breast: early lymph node spread to axilla
exam_pitfalls: Thinking mutation accumulation is time-dependent only (depends on selective pressure)
Assuming all tumours spread via bloodstream first (lymphatic spread often earlier)

key_facts: Clean surgery: single prophylactic dose at induction (goal: CPL of 1-1.5 hours before incision)
Clean-contaminated: continue 24h post-op (48h for cardiac surgery)
Choice depends on: wound type, local resistance patterns, allergy history
Re-dosing: if surgery exceeds 2 half-lives of antibiotic (e.g., cefazolin at 90 min)
clinical_scenarios: Routine cholecystectomy: cefazolin 1g IV at induction, that's it
Emergency appendicitis with perforation: requires prolonged course post-op, not just prophylaxis
exam_pitfalls: Giving 'prophylactic' antibiotics for >24 hours in clean surgery (becomes treatment)
Forgetting to re-dose in long cases

key_facts: Primary: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure
Life threats in primary: airway obstruction, tension pneumothorax, massive haemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
Secondary: head-to-toe systematic exam, back of patient rolled
Trauma ultrasound (FAST): pericardium, paracolic gutters, pouch of Douglas, pneumothorax
clinical_scenarios: Stab wound to chest: tension pneumo → immediate needle decompression before imaging
Car crush: bilateral leg crush → rhabdomyolysis, AKI risk
exam_pitfalls: Fixating on obvious wound while missing life threats in primary survey
Not rolling the patient to examine back (missed injuries)

key_facts: TNM: Tumour size/depth, Node involvement, Metastases
Stage grouping varies by cancer (stage 1 breast ≠ stage 1 colorectal)
Prognostic factors: grade, vascular invasion, margin status, lymph node ratio
Margin status: R0 (negative), R1 (microscopic positive), R2 (macroscopic positive)
clinical_scenarios: Colorectal cancer pT3N1M0 → stage IIIA → adjuvant chemo indicated
Breast cancer T1N0M0 Grade III HER2+ → might consider adjuvant despite stage I
exam_pitfalls: Confusing TNM with stage grouping (not 1:1 correlation)
Not considering other prognostic factors beyond TNM

key_facts: Capacity: understand relevant info, retain it, weigh it, communicate decision
Presumed competent until proven otherwise
Information: benefits, risks, alternatives, consequences of no treatment
Valid consent requires: capacity, information, voluntariness, no undue influence
clinical_scenarios: Confused elderly patient post-op: capacity assessed 6 hours post-op vs next morning
Jehovah's Witness refusing blood: competent refusal even if outcome worse
exam_pitfalls: Thinking age = incapacity (assess individual capacity, not age/diagnosis)
Forcing treatment on competent person refusing it (assault)
